1.title: The Plans Practice in Context
1.text: Welcome to Module five: The Plans Practice in Context. It covers the exam area The prince two practices. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Apply the plans practice: plan levels (project, stage, team, exception), project product description, work package description. Areas of focus of key roles. Effective planning and techniques. Analyze whether a planning approach is effective and fit for purpose considering the principles, the techniques and tailoring. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: The prince two practices (fifty-one percent). Exam format: an open-book scenario exam: one hundred fifty minutes, seventy marks, forty-two marks to pass. Validated against: the official prince two seven Practitioner syllabus (people cert), version seven point two.

1.title: Purpose, objectives and principles
1.text: Purpose, objectives and principles. The plans practice supports communication and control. A plan says what will be delivered, how, when, by whom and at what cost. Once the right level approves it, the plan becomes the baseline that progress is measured against. The practice serves these principles: focus on products (plan from the products, not from tasks), manage by stages (detail only for the stage ahead), manage by exception (tolerances sit inside the plan), learn from experience (past lessons feed estimates) and continued business justification (plan cost and time feed the business case).

1.title: Purpose, objectives and principles, continued
1.text: Purpose, objectives and principles. The figure shows this: The four levels of plan and who prepares and who approves each one. Exam tip: Match the plan to the management level. The board approves the project plan, stage plans and exception plans. The team manager owns the team plan. A scenario that gives the wrong person the wrong level of plan is a red flag.

1.title: The key management products
1.text: The key management products. Project plan. The whole project: major products, stages, cost, time, quality; updated at each stage boundary. Stage plan. One management stage in detail. Prepared by the project manager near the end of the previous stage; approved by the board. Team plan. An optional plan prepared by a team manager to deliver work packages, often in the team's own format. Exception plan. A plan that replaces the rest of the current plan when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded; the board requests it and approves it.

1.title: The key management products, continued
1.text: The key management products. Project product description. What the project as a whole must deliver, with the user quality expectations and acceptance criteria; agreed before detailed planning. Work package description. The work, product, standards, tolerances and reporting that the project manager agrees with a team manager before work starts. Exam tip: Work package description goes down to the team manager; exception plan goes up to the board. An exception plan replaces what remains of the current plan; it is not an addition.

1.title: Areas of focus of the key roles
1.text: Areas of focus of the key roles. Executive. Plans stay affordable and consistent with the business case. Senior user. Plans deliver what users need; agrees the project product description and acceptance criteria. Senior supplier. Plans are achievable with the supplier's resources and estimates. Project manager. Prepares project, stage and exception plans; writes work package descriptions. Team manager. Prepares team plans; agrees work packages and estimates. Project assurance. Checks plans are realistic and follow standards. Project support. Helps with planning tools, estimating data and plan upkeep. Where you are unsure of a detail, the exam habit is to check the book's table.

1.title: Effective planning and techniques
1.text: Effective planning and techniques. The planning approach is the agreed way of planning on this project: how many levels of plan, which tools, which estimating method and which standards. The syllabus names no separate product for it.

1.title: Effective planning and techniques, continued
1.text: Effective planning and techniques. Product-based planning. Write the project product description, draw the product breakdown structure, write product descriptions, draw the product flow diagram. Then find activities and dependencies. Estimating. Made with the people who will do the work, using past data and lessons; assumptions are stated. Scheduling. Uses dependencies and resource availability to show when, and the critical path. Tolerances. Set for the aspects of performance: corporate level sets project tolerance, the board sets stage tolerance, the project manager sets work package tolerance.

1.title: Effective planning and techniques, continued
1.text: Effective planning and techniques. Planning horizon. Detail for the current stage; outline for later stages. The plan as a control. The approved plan is the baseline; forecasts are compared with it. On Project Harbor a typical stage tolerance is plus or minus ten percent cost and two weeks time. Exam tip: Products first, activities second. If a plan starts with a task list and no product descriptions, it is not product-based planning, and acceptance criteria are probably missing.

1.title: Judging a scenario
1.text: Judging a scenario. Outline project plan; detailed plan for the current stage only (manage by stages). Detailed plans for every stage drawn up at the start and treated as fixed. Plans start from products and their descriptions (focus on products). A task list with no products, quality criteria or acceptance criteria. Every plan carries tolerances set by the level above (manage by exception). A single fixed date and cost, so every small slip goes to the board.

1.title: Judging a scenario, continued
1.text: Judging a scenario. Work package matches the stage plan and is agreed with the team manager. Work starts on a verbal request, or the work package quietly changes scope. Forecast breach: exception report, then an exception plan if the board asks. Project manager hides the breach, stretches the stage or writes a new plan unasked. Estimates made with the doers and past lessons (learn from experience). Estimates guessed by one person or never revisited. Project plan updated at each stage boundary and re-approved. Project plan never updated after approval.

1.title: Judging a scenario, continued
1.text: Judging a scenario. Tailoring. Small internal project. One combined plan; no team plan; short descriptions; decision recorded. Agile or hybrid delivery. Stage plan keeps time, cost and tolerances; sprint or release plans give the detail; scope flexes inside acceptance criteria. Large or multi-party project. Team plans for each supplier; dependencies between suppliers planned and integrated. Sustainability or data concerns. Plan includes sustainability and data measures and their tolerances. Exam tip: Tailoring changes the form of a plan, not the need for one. An answer that drops tolerances, baselines or board approval of stage plans because the project is small or agile is wrong.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. In Project Harbor, the build stage has a cost tolerance of plus or minus ten percent. Sam Okafor forecasts a fourteen percent overspend, drops the testing activities to recover the cost and carries on without telling anyone. Was this appropriate for the project manager? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: No, because the forecast breach must go to the board, which can request an exception plan. Manage by exception requires the forecast breach to be reported so the board decides; the plan cannot be quietly rewritten.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Project Harbor's initiation stage is ending. Sam Okafor is tempted to plan the build, pilot and rollout stages in full detail so the board feels certain. What should he do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Plan the build stage in detail and keep the later stages in outline in the project plan. Manage by stages and the planning horizon call for detail only for the next stage, with later stages in outline in the project plan.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Sam Okafor is about to authorize the next piece of build work to Wei Chen's team. Who is responsible for preparing the work package description that sets out the work, the product and the tolerances? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Sam Okafor, the project manager. The project manager prepares the work package description and agrees it with the team manager, who does not write the description of their own assignment.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Tomas Reyes wants the acceptance criteria for the whole online permit service agreed before the detailed plan is built. Which management product records them? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Project product description. The project product description holds what the whole project must deliver and the acceptance criteria; the others cover work, a stage or a team.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Sam Okafor sends Wei Chen a work package as an email with a task list and a due date only. There are no quality criteria, tolerances or reporting arrangements. Was this appropriate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: No, because it must state the product, quality criteria, tolerances and reporting and be agreed. A work package is a controlled agreement on product, standards, tolerances and reporting; a bare task list leaves both sides guessing.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Wei Chen's team delivers Project Harbor's build stage in two-week sprints from a prioritized backlog. What should Sam Okafor do about the stage plan? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Keep a stage plan with time, cost and tolerances, with sprint plans giving the detail. Tailoring adapts the form of planning for agile delivery, but the stage plan, tolerances and board control stay in place.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What does an exception plan replace? Answer: The remainder of the current plan, after a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded and the board asks for it. Question two. What is the first step of product-based planning? Answer: Write the project product description. Question three. Who sets the tolerance for a work package? Answer: The project manager, for the team manager.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Which plan is optional and prepared by a team manager? Answer: The team plan. Question five. How far ahead is detailed planning done in a staged project? Answer: For the current stage only; later stages stay in outline. Question six. What does a work package description tell a team manager? Answer: The work to do, the product to deliver, the standards, tolerances and reporting.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Plan levels: project plan, stage plan, team plan, exception plan. Exception plan: replaces the rest of a plan when tolerance is forecast to be exceeded. Project product description: what the whole project delivers, with acceptance criteria. Work package description: project manager to team manager: work, product, tolerances, reporting. Product-based planning: products first, then activities, estimates and schedule. Tolerances: corporate sets project, board sets stage, project manager sets work package. Tailoring: changes the form of plans, never drops tolerances or approval.
